# How To Calculate Your SAT Superscore: 2026 Guide + Tips


## TL;DR


An SAT superscore combines your highest Evidence-Based Reading and Writing (EBRW) score and your highest Math score from different test dates into one composite. Because colleges pull only your best section scores, your superscore can never go down, only up or stay the same. Over 1,000 colleges superscore the SAT, including all Ivy League schools. This makes retaking the SAT with targeted prep one of the highest-return strategies in college admissions.


Planning to retake the SAT? A[free SAT practice exam](https://miyagilabs.ai/sat/practice-exams) can help you identify which section needs the most work before test day.


> **Quick Answer: How Do You Calculate an SAT Superscore?**
>
>
> To calculate your SAT superscore, find your highest Reading and Writing score from every SAT you have taken, find your highest Math score from every SAT you have taken, and add the two scores together.
>
>
> **SAT superscore = highest Reading and Writing score + highest Math score**
>
>
> For example, if your highest Reading and Writing score is 740 and your highest Math score is 760, your SAT superscore is **1500** , even if you earned those two scores on different test dates.

## What Is an SAT Superscore?


An SAT superscore is a combined SAT score created by taking your highest Reading and Writing section score and highest Math section score from different SAT test dates and adding them together. Your superscore can be higher than your highest single-test total because the two section scores do not have to come from the same test date.


The SAT has two independently scored sections: Evidence-Based Reading and Writing (EBRW) and Math. Each section runs on a 200 to 800 scale, giving a total composite range of 400 to 1600.


When a college superscores, it takes the highest EBRW from any test date you’ve submitted and the highest Math from any test date, then adds them. That combined total is your SAT superscore.


Here’s a quick example:


EBRW

Composite

**740**

**1460**


Notice that neither single-sitting score reached 1460. The superscore pulled the best of both tests. This is the core advantage: your superscore is always equal to or higher than your best single-sitting composite. It can never decrease, no matter how a future test goes.


The College Board provides your individual SAT test scores and score reports, while colleges determine how they use those scores in admissions. If a college superscores, it can evaluate your highest section scores across eligible test dates according to its own policy.


If you want to build familiarity with the digital format before a retake, working through[SAT practice tests](https://miyagilabs.ai/sat/practice-tests) under realistic conditions is a solid starting point.


## SAT Superscore vs. Score Choice


This is where most students get confused. Score Choice and superscoring are not the same thing, and the distinction matters for your testing strategy.


**Score Choice** is a College Board feature that lets you choose which test *dates* to send. It controls what colleges see. If you send scores from a given test date, both sections from that sitting go together. You cannot cherry-pick just your Math from October and just your EBRW from March.


**Superscoring** is the college’s policy. It controls what they *use* . A superscore-friendly school will automatically pull your highest section scores from whichever test dates you’ve submitted and combine them.


So Score Choice is your filter, and superscoring is the college’s filter. They work in sequence: you decide what to send, then the college decides how to evaluate it.


Compass Prep, which maintains one of the most detailed trackers of college testing policies,[breaks schools into three tiers](https://www.compassprep.com/superscore-and-score-choice/) :


1.


**Require all scores** : The college explicitly requires every test score you’ve earned. Yale falls here.


2.


**Recommend all scores** : The college recommends (but doesn’t require) all scores and will superscore what you send.


3.


**Accept Score Choice** : The college lets you pick which dates to submit. Most schools fall here.


The practical takeaway: for superscore-friendly schools that accept Score Choice, send every test date that contains one of your highest section scores. For require-all schools, send everything and trust that the superscore policy works in your favor.


## How to Calculate Your SAT Superscore


There’s no official College Board “superscore calculator.” It’s straightforward arithmetic. Here’s the process:


1.


List every SAT test date and your section scores for each.


2.


Circle the highest EBRW score across all dates.


3.


Circle the highest Math score across all dates.


4.


Add them.


That total is your superscore.

710

680

**Superscore**


**690**


**740** = **1430**


In this example, the student’s best single-sitting composite was 1400 (June), but the superscore is 1430. Those 30 points can shift percentile rankings and open doors at competitive schools.

## SAT Superscore vs. Highest Composite Score


Your highest single-test SAT score and your SAT superscore are not necessarily the same.


Your highest composite score is the highest total you earned on one SAT test date.


Your superscore combines your highest Reading and Writing score and highest Math score across eligible test dates.


Because a superscore can combine section scores from different tests, your superscore can be higher than your highest single-test composite.

## Which Colleges Superscore the SAT?


Many colleges consider SAT superscores, but there is no universal superscoring policy. Each college determines how it evaluates SAT results, whether it accepts Score Choice, whether it requires all scores, and which test formats or administrations it considers eligible.


Because admissions policies can change between application cycles, students should verify the current policy directly with each college before deciding which SAT scores to submit.


### College SAT Superscoring Policy: What to Check

### Notable Policy Variations


**Georgetown University** is the most commonly cited school that does not formally accept superscores. However, Georgetown’s actual policy is more nuanced than most articles let on. According to their[admissions office](https://uadmissions.georgetown.edu/applying/preparation-process/) , Georgetown will consider the highest SAT Reading and Writing score and the highest Math score from the test or tests submitted. It does the same for ACT section scores. So while Georgetown doesn’t call it superscoring, they essentially run an internal superscore-like process. Practitioners on Reddit frequently flag this gap between Georgetown’s stated policy and its actual practice, and it causes real confusion.


**Yale:** Yale requires first-year and transfer applicants to submit ACT or SAT scores. Yale explicitly allows applicants to report superscored SAT results, meaning they can use their highest section scores across multiple SAT administrations. Yale also states that admitted students who enroll must provide official results matching their self-reported scores.


**Harvard** reviews your highest section scores from all dates submitted, which functions like a superscore in practice. But Harvard doesn’t frame it as a formal superscore policy, and it does accept Score Choice.


**Princeton:** Princeton's current policy is more nuanced than simply saying “Princeton does not superscore.” For the 2026–27 admission cycle, Princeton remains test optional, but students who submit SAT scores can have the highest individual SAT section results considered across sittings. Princeton specifically states that it does not superscore between the paper and digital SAT formats. Princeton plans to require SAT or ACT scores again beginning with the 2027–28 admission cycle.


The bottom line: always verify each school’s current policy on its admissions website. Policies change year to year. What was true when your older sibling applied may not be true now. ## SAT Superscore Strategy: How to Raise Yours


Superscoring creates what test prep strategists call “asymmetric upside.” Once you have a strong score locked in on one section, all your study effort can go toward the weaker section. The strong section is already banked. Even if it dips slightly on a retake, the college will use your earlier, higher score.


This changes how you should prepare.


### Target Your Weak Section


Say you scored 750 EBRW and 650 Math. You don’t need to split your study time 50/50. Pour your energy into Math. If your Math jumps to 710 on the retake (even if EBRW drops to 720), your superscore goes from 1400 to 1460.


This focused approach is the highest-ROI study strategy for retakers. To make it work, you need a clear diagnostic. Use a[SAT question bank](https://miyagilabs.ai/sat/question-bank) filtered by skill and difficulty to drill the specific areas dragging your weaker section down.


### The Data Supports Retaking


The College Board reports that[55% of high school juniors improved their scores](https://prepexpert.com/sat-retake-score-improvement/) when retaking as seniors, with an average improvement of about 40 points. Around 4% of retakers saw section score increases of 100 points or more.


Academic research backs this up even more strongly when superscoring is factored in. An[NBER study by Goodman et al.](https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w24945/w24945.pdf) found that retaking the SAT once improved students’ admissions-relevant superscores by nearly 0.3 standard deviations (roughly 90 points on the old 2400-point scale). For students who initially scored in the lower half of the SAT distribution, the superscore boost was even larger, around 0.4 standard deviations (approximately 120 points). Low-scoring students’ second-attempt superscores were 136 points higher on average, compared to 84 points for higher-scoring students.


These aren’t small numbers. A 90-point superscore improvement can shift a student from the 50th percentile to the 65th, or from a “maybe” pile to an “admit” pile at target schools.


### The Sweet Spot: 2 to 3 Attempts


Your first attempt establishes a baseline. The second attempt, after targeted practice, typically produces the largest score jump (30 to 100 points). A third attempt makes sense if you’re close to a target score or want to boost one specific section for superscoring purposes.


Beyond three attempts, diminishing returns set in. Your time has opportunity cost: college essays, extracurriculars, and the rest of your application all need attention. Allow 6 to 8 weeks between attempts for meaningful skill building. If you’re working with a compressed timeline, a[30-day SAT study plan](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/30-day-sat-study-plan) can help you focus your prep efficiently.


As of 2026,[standard SAT registration costs $68](https://blogs.learnq.ai/can-you-retake-the-sat/) . Students eligible for the College Board’s fee waiver can take the SAT twice for free.


### The Equity Angle


There’s a less-discussed dimension to superscoring worth noting. The same NBER research found that only about half of SAT-takers retake the exam, with even lower retake rates among low-income students and underrepresented minorities. Since retaking substantially improves superscores and increases four-year college enrollment rates, the researchers estimated that[eliminating disparities in retake rates](https://www.gse.harvard.edu/ideas/usable-knowledge/18/10/double-take) could close up to 10% of the income-based gap and up to 7% of the race-based gap in four-year college enrollment.


Superscoring is genuinely the most student-friendly admissions policy on the table. But its benefits flow disproportionately to students who can afford to test multiple times. If you qualify for fee waivers, use them.


## Common Misconceptions About SAT Superscoring


**“Colleges will penalize me for taking the SAT multiple times.”** They won’t. Colleges expect multiple attempts. More than half of juniors retake as seniors, and admissions offices are fully aware of this pattern.


**“My superscore could go down if I have a bad test day.”** Impossible. A superscore only uses your highest section scores. A lower score on a retake simply gets ignored in the superscore calculation.


**“I can superscore across SAT and ACT.”** No. Superscoring only works within the same test type. You cannot combine your best SAT Math with your best ACT English. These are entirely separate tests with different scoring systems. If you’re considering the ACT as well, our[ACT prep guide](https://miyagilabs.ai/act/prep) covers how ACT superscoring works separately.


**“Every college superscores.”** A small number don’t. Georgetown and Princeton are the most notable exceptions among highly selective schools, though Georgetown’s actual evaluation process resembles superscoring in practice.


**“The College Board doesn’t report superscores.”** It does. The College Board automatically includes your superscore on score reports. However, when you use the superscore reporting option, colleges will see full score reports from every test date used to create it, not just the two highest section scores in isolation.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### Can I superscore digital SAT and paper SAT results?


Yes. Both formats use the same two-section structure (EBRW and Math, each 200 to 800), so colleges and the College Board treat them as the same test for superscoring purposes.


### Does superscoring affect merit scholarships?


Some scholarship programs do use superscores when evaluating applicants, but this varies widely. Always check the specific scholarship’s requirements. Many state university merit awards are tied to your best composite, and superscoring can help there.


### How many times should I take the SAT if I’m planning to superscore?


Two to three times is the sweet spot for most students. The second attempt typically yields the biggest improvement, and a third can be useful for fine-tuning one section. Beyond that, your time is usually better spent on other parts of your application.


### Is there a fee to superscore?


No. Superscoring is automatic. The College Board calculates it and includes it on your score reports at no extra charge.


### What if a college requires all scores?


A few schools (like Yale) require you to submit scores from every test date. Even at these schools, the admissions office will superscore your results, pulling the best sections. Sending all scores at a superscore-friendly school is not a risk.


### Should I cancel a bad SAT score?


Generally, no. Since your superscore can only stay the same or go up, a low score on one section doesn’t hurt you at superscore-friendly schools. The exception would be a require-all-scores school where you’re concerned about optics, but even then, admissions officers understand score variation between test dates.


### Can I see my superscore before sending it?


Yes. Your College Board account shows your superscore alongside your individual test date scores. You can review it before deciding which scores to send.


### How long should I wait between SAT attempts?


Six to eight weeks is a good minimum. That gives you enough time for focused, deliberate practice on your weaker section rather than just retaking and hoping for the best.
